title: Filmmaker Marq Evans breaks down 'Capturing Bigfoot' documentary
byline: Chase Hutchinson from The Seattle Times
excerpt: “Capturing Bigfoot,” playing Sunday at SIFF, is a feature-length doc that uncovers significant revelations about the 1967 Patterson-Gimlin film and its origins.
content:
Marq Evans and Bigfoot go way back. At least, he and the film version do. 

The Yakima-born filmmaker has long been familiar with the infamous 1967 Patterson-Gimlin film, a three-minute-long 16mm short that concludes with what its creators claimed was the first footage of Bigfoot. Named for Roger Patterson (who died in 1972) and Robert “Bob” Gimlin, who both resided in Yakima, its story was passed down through generations.

“I know nothing about this story other than what my dad had told me as a kid,” Evans said. Now, the professor of documentary filmmaking at Bremerton’s Olympic College has made a definitive Bigfoot film of his own. 

“Capturing Bigfoot” is a feature-length documentary that uncovers significant revelations about the short, including never-before-seen footage that complicates its origins. However, while the film has become the subject of intense fascination from Bigfoot believers since premiering at this year’s SXSW Film Festival, it’s also a complex portrait of people still reeling from the short’s impact.

For Evans, this meant navigating relationships with people who had been profoundly close to this story, including Patterson’s son, Clint Patterson, who believed for much of his childhood that his dad truly discovered Bigfoot. Thus, the filmmaker wanted to treat everyone with respect and accept that, no matter what he showed them, many weren’t going to stop believing.

“Nobody wants to feel like they were tricked … so it’s hard for people to change their mind on something,” Evans said. “Clint came to realize, at one point, that (the footage) was fake, but he didn’t change his mind on how he felt about his dad.” Others, he said, dug in their heels because “they don’t want to be proven wrong.”

Similarly, Evans sees parallels between the documentary and a country often consumed by division, conspiracies and belief. He describes the elder Patterson in a “Picture Essay” series as the “first influencer” who “built a brand, monetized a passion and turned his critics into content, decades before that had a name." Some of the documentary subjects even speak with religious reverence about the original short.

“It’s faith, it’s wanting to believe in something,” Evans said. “Sometimes it’s about community, sometimes it's about just feeling not alone, or (that there are) other things out there.”

There are still differences among believers, and it's hard to fit them into neat boxes. Evans said some not only believe in Bigfoot, but claim to have had their own sightings, and then they become part of a community that provides them with validation for their beliefs. 

“There are other people who are just like, ‘Well, I believe in it, because I saw one,’ ” Evans said. “But either way, they’re now part of that community … and they feel like they’re together with those other people. Some people call them crazy, but (they say), ‘No, you see me.’ ”
